hints: Focus on oxidation numbers rather than just atoms moving around, as oxidation and reduction are all about change in oxidation state.
Chlorine starts as $\text{Cl}_2$ with oxidation state 0, then work out what it becomes in $\text{HOCl}$ and in $\text{Cl}^-$.
Check if hydrogen and oxygen change at all, then decide if the same element both gains and loses electrons in one reaction.
walkthrough:
**Recall what oxidised and reduced mean**

Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number (loss of electrons). Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number (gain of electrons).

Rule to use:
$$\text{increase in O.N. = oxidised, decrease in O.N. = reduced}$$

**Find the oxidation state of chlorine everywhere**

In $\text{Cl}_2$, each Cl is 0 because it is an uncombined element. This is our starting point.

In $\text{HOCl}$: H is +1 and O is -2, so Cl must be +1 to give a neutral molecule:
$$ (+1) + (-2) + \text{Cl} = 0 \text{ so Cl} = +1 $$

In $\text{Cl}^-$, Cl is -1.

**Compare start and end for chlorine**

One Cl atom goes $0 \to +1$. That is an increase, so it is oxidised.

The other Cl atom goes $0 \to -1$. That is a decrease, so it is reduced.

When the same element is both oxidised and reduced, we call it disproportionation.

**Check hydrogen (and oxygen) to be sure**

In $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, H is +1. In $\text{HOCl}$ and in $\text{H}^+$, H is still +1. No change, so no oxidation or reduction.

Oxygen is -2 in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and -2 in $\text{HOCl}$. No change either. So only chlorine changes, in both directions.

options.A: Correct. Chlorine starts at 0 in Cl2, goes up to +1 in HOCl (oxidised) and down to -1 in Cl- (reduced). This is a classic disproportionation reaction.
options.B: Incorrect. It is true that chlorine is oxidised (0 to +1), but it is also reduced (0 to -1 to form Cl-). This option misses half the story.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen stays at +1 in H2O, in HOCl and in H+. With no change in oxidation number, hydrogen is neither oxidised nor reduced.
options.D: Incorrect. Hydrogen does not change oxidation state at all, so it cannot be described as oxidised. Students sometimes confuse H+ formation with oxidation, but oxidation number is unchanged.
